sources.title: Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?
sources.text: Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large. He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares. But Huang’s image as a family man has been shattered as of Sunday. After the New York Times revealed at the end of October that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset who he had developed a close relationship with, he admitted in a letter to employees on Sunday that he had been having an affair. Initially , Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said there was nothing out of the ordinary about Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang , an executive at a Singaporean datacenter firm, Megaspeed. US government officials had suspected Huang of smuggling American chips into China, prompting those officials to surveil and monitor her, the Times first reported. In the course of that surveillance, officials allegedly determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had gotten close with the Nvidia leader. Nvidia’s board of directors have now launched an independent investigation about the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s relationship. “I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” Huang wrote in his letter. “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.” Megaspeed did not respond to a Guardian request for comment before publication. In his letter, Huang apologized to his family, acknowledging how much they’ve supported him. His wife, Mills, kept a relatively low profile and didn’t play a formal role at Nvidia. However, in a 2023 interview with the New Yorker, Huang shared that Mills had also worked in Silicon Valley as a microchips engineer before stepping away to raise their children. “Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support,” Huang wrote in his letter to employees. “They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.” Both his children now hold high ranking roles at the company, despite not initially pursuing careers in tech. His daughter, Madison, serves as the senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms, but got her start as a chef. She attended the Culinary Institute of America and Le Cordon Bleu before going to business school and transitioning to luxury marketing. She previously worked at LVMH – the parent company of Lous Vuitton. Spencer , for his part, now serves as the director of product for Robotics at Nvidia but spent much of his career as a consultant before joining his father’s company as a product manager. Before consulting, he owned and co-founded a craft cocktail bar in Taiwan. In his letter, Huang reiterated his commitment to Nvidia, saying he hoped to earn back his colleagues’ and employees’ trust. However, analysts and investors say there’s a chance he may be removed as CEO after the board’s investigation. “This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons,” said Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at investment bank Yorkville Ives. “There is clearly risk as discussed that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.” Ives said the family’s role at Nvidia adds some complexities for the board. “The board has to make its decision independent of the family spider web of Jensen and his family at Nvidia,” Ives told the Guardian. “It makes this a very complex situation for the board to navigate with the world watching.” Huang is to Nvidia what Steve Jobs was to Apple, said Ken Mahoney, the CEO and president of Mahoney Asset Management. “If you asked any Nvidia investor or anyone involved in tech and markets, would they like to see Jensen gone? Definitely not, but [Nvidia] would survive,” Mahoney said. “Losing Huang would introduce a lot of uncertainty, particularly given his influence over Nvidia’s strategy, culture, and relationships with major technology companies,” he continued. “The bigger question is whether a successor could maintain Huang’s strategic vision and ability to anticipate where the industry is heading, and how that new leader could be tested along the way if things become difficult.” Executive affairs or inappropriate relationships have recently unseated CEOs, according to executive recruiting and coaching firm Challenger Gray and Christmas. In 2024, the CEO of Astronomer was caught on a kiss cam with the company’s chief people officer, leading him to resign shortly after. Nestlé fired CEO Laurent Freixe for a relationship with a subordinate. Nvidia offers a more complex picture. On one hand, Huang’s affair is not just a matter morals or ethics, there are potential national security concerns. On the other, Huang is core to the DNA of Nvidia which in turn is the bedrock of the entire AI industry – an industry upon which the economy relies greatly. Nvidia shares fell 7.5% as soon as the stock market opened, wiping over $330bn off the company’s value. “When the CEO of the most valuable company in the world is tied to a counterintelligence investigation because of a personal relationship, every board in America should be paying attention,” said

sources.title: Nvidia board member Stephen Neal could play big role in probe of CEO Jensen Huang
sources.text: Nvidia's investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy may hinge on decisions by company board member Stephen Neal , a longtime white-collar defense attorney whose extensive resume includes dealing with corporate scandals. Neal, the former CEO of the Cooley law firm, is Nvidia's lead independent director and head of corporate governance. Nvidia has not named the investigators who will probe the allegations surrounding Huang, but the company has said its board is leading the probe with help from outside counsel. Neal's experience makes him a likely key figure in the investigation. Nvidia's board has said there is "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised" by Huang's admitted affair with Alice Huang, who had been an executive with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. China dismissed U.S. intelligence conclusions that Alice Huang was a spy, which were first reported by The New York Times . Jensen Huang, one of the most powerful businessmen in the artificial intelligence boom, has said he would "cooperate fully" with the investigation. Nvidia's board has 10 independent members, including a former president of Taco Bell , a former Eli Lilly executive, and a former vice chairman from Goldman Sachs . Neal has litigated cases across securities, bankruptcies, antitrust, takeovers and more, according to his Cooley bio. And he's conducted several investigations for multiple boards of directors, including at General Motors , where he advised the company in disputes with Ross Perot. Neal has also conducted several investigations for committees of directors and independent directors, though most of those client names are confidential. He's also handled investigations with the Securities and Exchange Commission for both corporations and individuals. When he joined Nvidia, Neal was also the chairman of the board of directors at Levi Strauss . He stepped down in 2021 after reaching the mandatory board retirement age of 72, the company said at the time. The retailer did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Monday. Neal joined Nvidia's board in 2019. He is chairman emeritus and senior counsel at Cooley, and was the firm's CEO from 2001 to 2008. Neal did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Neal's past clients include Elizabeth Holmes , the convicted fraudster who founded the blood-testing startup Theranos, and late financier Charles Keating Jr . Neal and other Cooley lawyers represented Holmes in a class-action civil lawsuit in Arizona federal court over Theranos' blood-testing services, which produced bogus results. In September 2019, Neal and his colleagues asked to be removed from the case because Holmes could not pay their legal bills. A judge granted that withdrawal motion less than two months later. In 1989, Neal was hired to represent Keating, who had become the face of the massive savings and loan scandal in the United States as head of American Continental, which owned the California-based thrift Lincoln Savings & Loan. Keating's campaign contributions to five U.S. senators — none of whom were charged with wrongdoing — earned them the notorious sobriquet "The Keating Five." Keating was sentenced in 1992 to up to 10 years in prison by Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Lance Ito for an extensive fraud. Ito later gained fame as the judge in O.J. Simpson's murder trial. Keating ended up serving less than five years after that conviction and a federal one were overturned on appeal. Neal represented Keating in his efforts to overturn his convictions. In a 1997 article about Keating, Time magazine called Neal "the legal Houdini behind his release." Neal also has ties in and around Silicon Valley. In November 2022, in the wake of the collapse of the $32 billion cryptocurrency firm FTX, the company's founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, nominated Neal to serve as chairman of the board of FTX Trading, the FTX-affiliated hedge fund Alameda Research, and a third affiliate, West Realm Shires, as part of a Chapter 11 bankruptcy petition. But Cooley said Neal was "unable to serve in" those positions, Business Insider reported at the time. Neal received his law degree from Stanford, where Bankman-Fried's parents had been law professors. Neal is also chairperson of the trust for Meta's Oversight Board , which is responsible for examining whether Meta's decisions to remove or leave up content on Facebook, Instagram or Threads were in line with the company's policies and values. And on Tuesday, the journalist Theo Baker, whose articles as a freshman reporter on The Stanford Daily at Stanford University about allegations against that school's president Marc Tessier-Lavinge led to his resignation, said in an X post that Tessier-Lavinge had hired Neal "to try to stop my reporting on allegations of research misconduct from coming out." Cooley's history with Nvidia goes back decades. The law firm said it incorporated the company in 1993 and has served as its principal outside corporate and litigation counsel for roughly three decades. Cooley handled Nvidia's initial public offering in 1999. Investors will be closely watching the investigation, and its emphasis on independence, as the process unfolds, according to Brayden King, a professor of management and organizations at Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management. "You definitely want somebody leading it who people can look at and say, 'OK, we believe this is a report that we can fully believe and trust that the outcome is the right outcome,'" King said. "That's what investors are looking for. They just don't like the instability that comes with all of this." King said the Nvidia investigation sits at a unique intersection of Wall Street and Washington, where the company is likely navigating its next steps to try to appease both groups. sources.title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
sources.text: Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested. Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested. As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket. Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI. “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.” Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute. For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged. Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI. Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge . “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.” It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China. Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says. Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions. Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge . “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.” The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says. Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan. “When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.” But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding

sources.title: ‘Stay, with less’: Why Nvidia’s board may rein in Jensen Huang rather than fire him
sources.text: Jensen Huang has acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese spy . On Sunday, the same day it opened an independent investigation, Nvidia’s board said it had confidence in its CEO. Investors were less sure. Nvidia shares fell as much as 8.8% on Monday and closed down about 4.3%, wiping roughly $190 billion off the market value of a company that ranked as the most valuable on the 2026 Fortune 500 . For most CEOs, that sounds like the kind of week that ends with a resignation letter. But at Nvidia, even removing the CEO could be complicated. “In most cases of scandal at major corporations, the CEO is either replaced or put on leave while investigations are carried out and appropriate responses decided,” Jo-Ellen Pozner, an associate professor of management at Santa Clara University’s Leavey School of Business, told Fortune . Nvidia’s board faces two problems. It may be reluctant to force out the man who built the company, and even if it wanted to, there is no obvious successor. “I don’t expect a ‘stay or go’ decision. It will be more like a ‘stay, with less,’” Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor of accounting at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business, told Fortune . Schloetzer said the board could appoint a clear second-in-command, communicate more openly about succession planning, and reshuffle board seats to signal stronger oversight. Huang would remain CEO, but under closer supervision At a typical large corporation, the board oversees the CEO and succession planning, while layers of senior management provide potential replacements. Nvidia operates differently. Huang has built an unusually flat management structure , with dozens of direct reports and few layers of hierarchy. Pozner calls it “an extremely unusual organizational structure.” It has kept Huang at the center of the company since its founding in 1993. “I also imagine that he did it in part to prevent politics and political factions within the organization,” Pozner said. That model can work well at a small organization, she explained, but Nvidia has outgrown it. “There needs to be disagreements and productive conflict and things like that,” she added. Over time, she said, the structure “had the effect of suppressing the emergence of potential successors, probably diminishing conflict and consolidating power in the hands of Jensen Huang.” Nvidia has not publicly identified a successor . Pozner said promoting an insider would be risky because investors, regulators and business partners would be looking for credibility and stability. That leaves bringing in an outsider, which carries risks of its own. Finding a replacement is only half the problem. The other half is whether Nvidia’s board would be willing to remove Huang at all. Nvidia has no board chair, a position typically responsible for leading the board and overseeing management. Instead, Huang works with lead independent director Stephen Neal to set board meeting agendas, while management prepares the information presented to directors, according to the company’s filings. Neal can also convene meetings of independent directors without Huang. Of Nvidia’s 11 board members, three, including Huang, have served continuously since the company’s founding in 1993, while another joined in 1997. A fifth director, Mark Stevens, served from 1993 to 2006 before returning in 2008, according to the company’s 2026 proxy statement . Although Nvidia classifies all directors other than Huang as independent, Pozner questioned whether their longstanding relationships and the company’s governance structure could affect their willingness to hold him accountable. “They’ve become billionaires because of their affiliation and ownership of this company. And just working together with the same CEO since the inception of the organization makes it impossible for them to act as outsiders,” she said. The board’s Sunday statement said a committee of independent directors, with help from outside counsel, would oversee the investigation. It said it had expressed confidence in Huang before that work was completed and that the board had no reason to believe national security or Nvidia’s secrets had been compromised. “It is unclear that a captive board like this—which in some ways is not unlike Tesla’s—has the heart to question, censure, or sanction Huang, and it is doubtful that it has taken succession planning very seriously,” Pozner said. The controversy has also produced something rare in Washington: bipartisan agreement. On Monday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.) and Sen. Jim Banks (R., Ind.) issued a joint statement calling for answers from Nvidia and tighter restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. Nvidia and Huang are also being sued in a proposed shareholder class action that alleges they misled investors about Huang’s ties to Alice Huang. And President Trump said the FBI was looking into the nature of the relationship. For now, Nvidia is standing behind its CEO. A company spokesperson told Axios that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO without interruption. Some investors are equally reluctant to see him go. Michael Monaghan, a partner at Founder ETFs, told Axios that his firm would sell its Nvidia holdings if Huang departed, calling him in some ways “irreplaceable.” “We don’t really believe there is such a thing as succession in these massive founder-led companies,” Monaghan said. Prediction markets lean the same way: Polymarket traders put the odds of Huang resigning or being removed by year-end at 16%, Fortune reported . Keeping Huang doesn’t necessarily mean business as usual. A failure to be candid with the board, however, could still cost Huang his job. “Boards remove CEOs over candor issues,” Schloetzer said. “What did he tell the directors, and when? sources.title: NVIDIA shareholders are suing the company and CEO Jensen Huang
sources.text: The company’s shares have plummeted in response to the exec’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The unfolding drama around NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman now accused of being a spy for the Chinese government may be getting its first courtroom chapter. A shareholder in the computing giant has sued accusing NVIDIA and Huang of misleading investors about the nature of the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Taiwanese company Megaspeed who is now suspected of being an espionage asset for China. Huang is a common surname; The pair are not related. Mark Kistenmacher filed the complaint and is seeking class action status for anyone who purchased NVIDIA shares between October 9 and November 8. The first date is when The New York Times published a story on NVIDIA and Megaspeed detailing a connection between the pair, which was rebuffed by NVIDIA as a routine business relationship; the second date is when the NVIDIA founder admitted to an affair and the company publicly disclosed that it was launching its own investigation into whether its top exec had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. In the interim, The New York Times published an in-depth feature on October 29 claiming that the NVIDIA CEO had become the subject of a suspected Chinese intelligence action. The piece cites NVIDIA representative John Rizzo, who said, "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." This statement, the lawsuit alleges, was not true. The company's shares have dropped in the fallout of the allegations, with NVIDIA on track to lose more than $470 billion in market value over the past two days. "As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages," the complaint states.

sources.title: NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 has presets you should know about
sources.text: Like it or lump it, there's no getting away from upscalers if you're a PC gamer who loves modern AAA titles. For those on the NVIDIA side of the divide, the company's Deep Learning Super Sampling tech is increasingly needed if you want to run graphically demanding games at high frame rates with ray tracing whacked all the way up. If you regularly deploy DLSS 4.5 in games, there are tweaks you can make through the NVIDIA app to squeeze better performance and cleaner visuals from your favorite titles. The internet remains very upset about NVIDIA's DLSS 5 , and rightfully so. Thankfully, DLSS 4.5 is focused purely on delivering the best balance between image quality and performance, not needlessly yassifying in-game character models. We'll run you through DLSS 4.5's K, L, and M presets, how they compare to each other, and what hardware is best suited to each. We'll also touch on in-app tweaks you can make to reduce visual glitches that may occur if you enable frame generation. There's no real "best" preset, per se. It's more a case of judging what the most suitable option is for striking the right balance between visual quality and performance, which ties into how powerful your GPU is. To switch between DLSS 4.5's various presets via the app, go to Graphics > Global Settings > DLSS Override – Model Presets . First up, preset K has been designed to deliver the best image quality, so it should be the go-to for folks who own the highest-end gaming PCs (more on that shortly). If you're gaming on more modest hardware, presets M and L have been tailored towards DLSS 4.5 Performance and Ultra Performance modes respectively. If you're playing on, say, an RTX 4070, opting for preset M should deliver attractive results without hitting your frame rates too hard. Upscaling from an internal resolution of 1080p, this option produces results that can look really pleasing on a 4K screen thanks to strong image stability. Gamers who want to play the best PC games on either RTX 30 or 20 Series cards would be better off selecting preset L, especially if the title in question has ray tracing. Sure, the image won't be quite as stable as M, meaning you're likely to encounter ghosting issues when the camera is moving around quickly in games. Still, preset L can deliver convincingly high resolution results on 1440p and 4K monitors. That's impressive, considering DLSS 4.5 is upscaling from an internal 720p resolution. In short, if you own bleeding edge PC components, preset K will produce the most eye-arousing results. The performance-focused M is great for mid-range gaming PCs and does a good job upscaling from 1080p. For aging rigs, preset L delivers the most performance bang for your buck and looks pretty decent doing so. Whether you own a 4K monitor or have your PC hooked up to your main living room TV like I do, playing AAA games on a beefy rig in Ultra HD is pretty glorious. Provided your GPU and CPU are up to the task, DLSS 4.5's preset K is best placed to deliver eye-rubbing 2160p results. Though preset M does a commendable job upscaling from 1080p, the higher baseline resolutions that K is working with produces image quality that's closer to native 4K output. Once you choose K from the NVIDIA app's model presets menu, you can further tailor the visual experience you're hoping to obtain by hopping to "DLSS Override – Super Resolution Mode". Here, you're best choosing either DLAA, Quality or Balanced to hit a high level of image quality. However, since DLAA outputs at 100% resolution, you really need an expensive 50 Series GPU with this option if you want to avoid tanking frame rates in demanding modern games. The Quality and Balanced options are obviously less taxing than rendering games at native output. The former upscales from 1440p (that's around 66.7% of a native 4K image), while the latter scales from a baseline 2227 x 1253 pixels (about 58% of 4K). You can also set a custom input resolution from this sub menu. Whenever possible, I go with DLAA, as it provides the best form of anti-aliasing to all but eliminate most in-game jaggies. That said, I do own an RTX 5090. For most folks with decent GPUs, pairing preset K with Balanced mode will provide strong performance with image quality that should look great on most 4K displays. Team Green's Multi Frame Generation tech is capable of delivering hugely impressive FPS numbers... with a couple of caveats. Though you can run the likes of Cyberpunk 2077 at over 200 FPS with full path tracing when the x6 multiplier is enabled, latency can increase significantly, while visual glitches may also occur. To reduce the latter issue, it's best to tweak settings in the Frame Generation tab of the DLSS Override – Model Presets section. Not to be confused with the previously mentioned K, L, and M presets, frame generation has its own unique options to help smooth out image quality. By default, the app chooses the "Use 3D app setting", while also placing an asterisk next to the Recommended preset with the disclaimer this option should provide the best balance between optimal quality and performance in most cases. You also have the choice of presets A and B. In most instances, it's the latter you should go with. However you feel about NVIDIA's DLSS 4.5 Multi Frame Generation tech and its AI-assisted frames, it is capable of delivering game-changing performance in titles that push path-tracing hard, such as Resident Evil Requiem . However, the frame gen preset you choose can have a substantial impact on what you see onscreen. In my experience, choosing the older A preset can cause obvious visual bugs. In the case of Requiem or 007 First Light, this most commonly manifests as a distracting shimmering effect around 2D elements, like onscreen icons. When I've encountered these ugly issues, swapping from preset A to the more recent B variant has generally cleaned up these problems completely, or at least made them less visible. sources.text: Today Anthropic, PBC launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock. The proposed offering consists of 825,000,000 shares of Class A common stock. Of these, 801,351,354 shares are being offered by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares are being offered by certain existing stockholders. Anthropic will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders. Anthropic also expects to grant the underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to an additional 123,750,000 shares of its Class A common stock. The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” The proposed offering will be made only by means of a prospectus. Copies of the preliminary prospectus may be obtained from: Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 200 West Street, New York, NY 10282, by telephone at (866) 471-2526, or by email at prospectus-ny@ny.email.gs.com; or Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 180 Varick Street, 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10014. sources.title: Anthropic launches IPO roadshow with $64B fundraising goal
sources.text: Anthropic PBC today kicked off the roadshow for its upcoming initial public offering. An IPO roadshow is a series of promotional events aimed at persuading institutional investors to buy shares. Anthropic plans to sell 825 million units of common stock for $70 to $78 per share, which works out to $64.35 billion at the top end of the range. About 23 million of the shares will be offered by the company’s seven co-founders, who are each set to make $250 million. The funding haul could increase significantly if the banks underwriting the IPO exercise their over-allotment option. Anthropic will enable them to buy nearly 124 million shares within 30 days of the IPO. At the top end of the company’s target pricing, that stock would be worth $965 million. Anthropic logged $17 billion in revenue and a $536 million operating loss last quarter. Its pitch to roadshow participants will likely emphasize its rapid growth. According to the company’s IPO filing, it generated about seven times more revenue during the first nine months of the year than in all of 2025. Anthropic’s strategy for maintaining its sales growth doesn’t rely solely on new model releases. It’s also building out a portfolio of tools that make its models easier to use. The three newest additions to the lineup made their debut today alongside the launch of the IPO roadshow. The first offering, Claude Meetings, is an artificial intelligence assistant designed for video conferences. Workers can use it to retrieve information from business applications and generate project plans. They can then use Claude Whiteboard, the second tool that Anthropic debuted today, to brainstorm the AI-generated content and make revisions. The company’s third new product is also designed for productivity tasks. Claude Sheets is a spreadsheet editor with a natural language interface. It can be used together with Claude Data, an existing Anthropic offering previously known as Claude Dashboards that moved into general availability today. It can automatically turn Claude-generated spreadsheets and other files into dashboards. Goldman Sachs, one of the IPO’s lead underwriters, reportedly estimates that Anthropic will end the year with about $52 billion in revenue. According to the Financial Times , the bank expects that number to grow more than tenfold by 2030. Goldman Sachs reportedly believes Anthropic will achieve positive free cash flow in the same time frame. Free cash flow is a profitability metric that measures a company’s revenue minus operating expenses. In conjunction with Anthropic’s IPO, seven of its top suppliers will buy $26 billion worth of shares through a private placement. The group includes Nvidia Corp., Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Broadcom Inc., Google LLC, Micron Technology Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Reuters reported that TSMC also plans to invest $500 million in OpenAI Group PBC’s IPO. Anthropic is expected to price its shares on Nov. 18. The company will list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. sources.title: Trump stands by Nvidia boss Jensen Huang despite spy scandal, but FBI is investigating
sources.text: The revelations this weekend that Nvidia Corp. boss Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman who has been accused of working for Chinese intelligence have now ensnared U.S. President Donald Trump, raising further questions about national security. At the same time, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said it’s looking into the affair, meaning it’s likely to get continuing attention in coming weeks or longer. Nvidia said it has launched an investigation into Chief Executive Huang’s actions after he admitted to cheating on his wife with a woman known as Alice Huang (no relation), who serves as the CEO of a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed . U.S. intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang has been feeding information about Huang and the chipmaker’s plans to the Chinese government. And though Trump was informed of the possible infiltration, he has continued working with Nvidia and Huang on domestic policy issues related to technology and artificial intelligence, which have become of vital importance to the U.S. economy. Huang has spent the last two years cultivating a close relationship with Trump, gaining extraordinary access to America’s top decision-maker and influence over the country’s AI strategy. He has gone from being virtually unknown to the president to being a key member of a cadre of technology industry executives accompanying him on trips aboard Air Force One, including a visit to China in May. He has come to be seen as a major ally of Trump, attending numerous White House events while repeatedly praising his policies. Notably, his company made a $25 million donation to the president’s gaudy ballroom project, becoming its top corporate contributor alongside Apple Inc. Those efforts seem to have gone a long way toward getting Huang into the president’s good graces, and it seems to have paid off for the company. Last year, after months of lobbying from Huang and Nvidia, the Trump administration agreed that it could sell more advanced chips to China that were previously banned from being exported to the country. Though that decision was widely known, it seems that the Trump administration has intervened in other ways to protect Nvidia’s interests. Earlier today, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed, which was suspected of smuggling banned chips into China, was abruptly canceled after receiving an email from Nvidia’s general counsel. Commerce official Jeff Kessler, who was nominated for the role by Trump, reportedly gave Nvidia permission to contact the investigation team and mention his name, which goes against standard protocol. Investigators had grown suspicious that Megaspeed was essentially just a front for smuggling embargoed Nvidia chips into China, but the correspondence from Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter kicked off a kerfuffle that ultimately led to the investigation being transferred to the Department of Justice. But Trump defended Huang late on Sunday, stating that the Nvidia boss is an “honorable guy” who has not committed any wrongdoing. The president had been briefed about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation as far back as October 2025, but decided not to do anything , according to the Times. “I haven’t heard that he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody, but, you know, so does everybody else.” Trump continued to defend Huang on Monday when quizzed about the situation again, before revealing that the Federal Bureau of Investigation is also looking into his relationship with the suspected spy. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” he said at a White House briefing. Despite the apparent protection afforded by Trump, Huang appears to be taking no chances. A report in Wired said today that the Nvidia boss has hired the services of a public relations firm called Heller that specializes in handling public scandals. Rise Heller, the firm’s founder, has developed a reputation for helping powerful men sidestep allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies. She previously represented clients including the former Congressman Anthony Weiner, the writer Jeffrey Toobin and the chef Mario Batali, Wired reported. Tech industry personalities have also leapt to Huang’s defense. Shaun Maguire, a partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital said in a post on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” and stressed that although he did something “incredibly dumb,” he believes there was “no bad intention.” Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk later shared Maguire’s post, saying he agrees with all of it. However, no intervention has managed to protect Nvidia’s stock, which slid more than 4% on Monday , wiping around $190 billion off of the company’s valuation. Nvidia is scheduled to hold its next financial earnings call on Nov. 17, in which Huang is likely to face some very difficult questions — if he is on the call as has been customary.
